does: Coats every piece evenly with a dressing or a sauce by lifting and turning.

intro.what: Tossing lifts and turns food so dressing coats the pieces lightly and evenly.
intro.why: It teaches you to distribute a small addition without crushing delicate ingredients.

how: Put the food in a bowl far larger than it needs.
Add the dressing a little at a time, around the edge and not on top.
Lift from the bottom and let the pieces fall, with clean hands or a pair of spoons.
Taste a piece and adjust before serving.

cues.text: Every piece glistens, and nothing pools in the bottom of the bowl.

mistakes.mistake: Dressing leaves long before serving, so that the acid and salt make them limp.
Pouring on all the dressing at once, which drowns the food.
mistakes.fix: Add it in stages and stop when everything is lightly coated.

quiz.question: What is the aim when tossing with dressing?
choices: Dressing pooled beneath dry upper pieces.
Light even coating across the pieces.
A dense pile crushed into the dressing.
quiz.because: Lifting from below brings undressed surfaces into contact without heavy stirring.

quiz.question: Why choose a bowl with plenty of room?
choices: To keep the dressing away from the food.
To make pressing the leaves harder easier.
To lift and turn without compressing or spilling the food.
quiz.because: Space permits gentle movement that distributes dressing while preserving delicate pieces.

quiz.question: Which appearance suggests enough dressing?
choices: Pieces glisten without a pool at the bottom.
Dry patches remain above a deep puddle.
Dressing runs off every piece in streams.
quiz.because: A light sheen indicates coating without excess free dressing.

quiz.question: Leaves turned limp before service. What would you change next time?
choices: Dress them earlier and leave them longer.
Toss them at the last moment.
Squeeze them harder into the dressing.
quiz.because: Salt and acid act on dressed leaves over time, so late tossing better preserves their texture.
